transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-04 15:00 UTC • Duration: 46m
Attendees: Alex Chen, Maya Patel, Jordan Lee (Redwood); Tom Rinehart, Priya Singh, Luis Gomez, Sara Albright (Acadia)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um quick agenda — we want to walk through our recommended key topology for multi-tenant rate controls, show the console demo for org/project key branching, and surface some Optimize tips for your traffic patterns.
[00:22] Tom Rinehart: Great, we had a quick pre-note — our spikes come from batch exports and checkout events, plus peak campaigns. Latency matters for checkout flows.
[00:36] Maya Patel: Totally. Can you share a rough RPS and the burst profile, Tom? even ballpark helps.
[00:45] Priya Singh: We're seeing about 250 rps baseline, with bursts to 1.2k for short windows (a few mins) during sales. Most calls are generation requests at seq length ~380 tokens.
[01:10] Jordan Lee: Okay that maps to a typical mid-size ecomm. We'll show two patterns: 1) org-key first-class with project keys for teams; 2) project-only with sticky routing. There are tradeoffs re: quota segmentation and sticky caches.
[01:50] Alex Chen: Quick callout — when people say sticky routing they mean affinity to the same backend so KV cache and prefix cache warm up, yes. We do keep prefix cache when the key pins to the same instance group.
[02:15] Luis Gomez: Security question — how does KMS and audit logging work if we go Private? we need HSM integration for keys and detailed audit trail.
[02:30] Maya Patel: Good question. For Private, you can bring your KMS or HSM and we'll integrate via our key-provider hooks, plus the control plane emits audit logs to your S3/syslog. We'll send the SOC2 excerpt after.
[02:56] Alex Chen: Ok demo time — opening console. (typing noises) Sorry the demo is a little laggy on my end.
[03:12] [Screen-share] Maya Patel: Here's the org page — you can create org-level quota lanes, attach project keys under projects, and configure burst buckets that live above project quotas. So if Acadia wants a global burst pool for marketing campaigns you can configure that.
[03:40] Tom Rinehart: If we do a global burst pool does that risk starving checkout traffic?
[03:48] Jordan Lee: We recommend priority lanes — you mark checkout as high-priority route and create reserved tokens for that project. Burst pool is available for non-critical routes only, or you can set hard-guards.
[04:20] Priya Singh: How does the system backpressure? like if the cluster is saturated do requests queue or do you drop?
[04:32] Maya Patel: We implement graceful backpressure — adaptive immediate responses when latency SLOs can't be kept: short-circuit errors with retry-after headers and optional queued windows if you enable the buffering layer. It depends on your deployment (Hosted vs Dedicated has different knobs).
[05:05] Tom Rinehart: Can we test a canary for a new model without blowing our quotas? we want to ramp slowly per project.
[05:16] Alex Chen: Yes canary rollouts are first-class in the console — you can route X% of traffic to new model variant per project, and tie that to a quota shard. We'll show the rollout policy UI.
[05:40] [06:00] Maya Patel: switching to Optimize — Optimize analyzes your sequence length distribution and recommends batching and quant profiles. For your 380 token average, we might suggest dynamic batching window to reduce per-token cost and a 4-bit quant for non-regeneration heavy flows.
[06:30] Priya Singh: 4-bit quant — does that risk quality regressions for our checkout assistant?
[06:42] Jordan Lee: It can, yes. Optimize ties to evaluation traces — we run your prompt set and show expected quality delta. You can allow quant only on background tasks like recommendations and keep checkout on full precision.
[07:10] Luis Gomez: On compliance, do your logs include tokenized outputs or full text? we can't store PII.
[07:21] Maya Patel: We support filtering at the routing layer — you can redact tokens before logs are emitted. For Private installs you entirely control log retention and redaction.
[07:48] Tom Rinehart: We're considering Hosted for dev and Dedicated for prod. What does dedicated mean for quotas?
[07:58] Alex Chen: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and isolated billing units. Quotas are enforced per tenancy but you still get org/project keys for logical routing. Dedicated also allows higher burst ceilings with capacity commitments.
[08:25] Priya Singh: Walk me through an example — marketing sends a campaign spike hitting the org key, what enforces checkout priority?
[08:37] Jordan Lee: You configure priority policies: reserved lanes, hard caps, and fallback models. If marketing hits the burst pool, traffic is consumed there; when pool is depleted, non-priority requests are rate-limited first. Checkout keys are pinned to a reserved lane with guaranteed token allotment.
[09:00] [09:35] Alex Chen: Quick note on billing segmentation — project keys let you bill per team or customer. Org keys are useful for global controls but can complicate per-project chargebacks.
[09:52] Priya Singh: We need to keep a clean cost mapping. Probably per-project billing is better for us.
[10:05] Maya Patel: Good, then make project keys the billing anchor and keep an org-level guard for policy enforcement.
[10:30] [11:00] Tom Rinehart: Any third-party throttle behaviors we should be aware of — e.g., our API gateway may retry aggressively.
[11:12] Jordan Lee: Recommend idempotency keys and client-side backoff. We also provide a token-based retry header that helps you distinguish client retries from genuine load.
[11:45] Priya Singh: Can we model our burst and see how fairshare would behave?
[11:55] Maya Patel: Yup. Console has a simulator — you can upload a CSV with traffic trace and run multiple policy scenarios. Let's demo a quick sim. (uploads file)
[12:18] [12:40] Maya Patel: Running sim now — shows checkout preserved, marketing throttled after 45s, overall tail latency reduced. Note the sim assumes 8 GPU nodes; we'll adjust if your committed capacity is different.
[13:05] Tom Rinehart: Nice. If we go Private, what's the network topology requirement? we have strict egress rules.
[13:18] Alex Chen: Private supports VPC peering, private link and on-prem with air-gapped control plane options. For strict egress you can configure all egress to go through your proxy. We'll share architecture doc.
[13:45] Luis Gomez: SSO and RBAC — we need SAML + SCIM integration and role separation for billing vs infra.
[13:56] Maya Patel: We have SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and granular RBAC. For Dedicated/Private, you can map roles to your internal groups.
[14:20] Priya Singh: One of our concerns is cache warm-up — during canary we might hit cold KV caches and latency spikes. Any mitigations?
[14:33] Jordan Lee: Two mitigations: sticky routing so the same project key hits warmed instances, and a pre-warm API that can populate KV cache using historical prefixes. There's also a read-through cache layer.
[15:00] Tom Rinehart: If we shard project keys across multiple backend pools for isolation, does that increase cost?
[15:12] Alex Chen: It can, because you're reserving capacity per pool. There's a tradeoff between isolation and unit economics. Optimize can run cost projections for proposed topologies.
[15:40] [16:05] Maya Patel: show console: creating a project key, attaching route, setting quota — note you can set per-minute concurrency, per-day token caps, and stash a burst bucket.
[16:30] Priya Singh: Can we export the quota usage via API for our billing system?
[16:39] Jordan Lee: Yes there's billing endpoints and webhook support for threshold alerts. We'll send API docs.
[17:00] Tom Rinehart: On the security side, how are keys rotated?
[17:09] Maya Patel: Keys rotate via our key manager; for Private you can enforce rotation policies through your KMS. We can do automated rotation or forced rotation windows.
[17:38] Priya Singh: Are there guardrails to prevent a compromised project key from draining the burst pool?
[17:48] Alex Chen: Yes you can set per-key rate caps, ephemeral tokens, and enforce IP whitelists. Also alerting on abnormal usage patterns via anomaly detection.
[18:10] [18:40] Tom Rinehart: Competitor question — we've looked at RivetAI and CloudInfer; how do you compare on predictable latency and cost?
[18:52] Jordan Lee: Our differentiation is production-first routing + Optimize recommendations. We focus on predictable tail latency and showing unit economics for each routing policy. RivetAI focuses on model ops; CloudInfer emphasizes raw throughput but less on tenant-level controls.
[19:20] Priya Singh: Any limits on how many project keys we can create?
[19:28] Maya Patel: Practically no hard limit — we recommend logical groupings to avoid performance overhead; we'll size your control plane accordingly.
[19:55] [20:10] Alex Chen: Let's demo a failure mode — I'll simulate a cluster node failure and show fallback model routing. (console actions)
[20:35] Maya Patel: Fallback policy will transparently route to a compatible lower-cost model variant and mark the request with fallback metadata in the trace so you can evaluate degraded outputs in logs.
[21:05] Luis Gomez: Do you keep model outputs in traces? again PII concern.
[21:14] Maya Patel: By default we keep traces for debugging but you can disable retention or redact outputs. For enterprise customers we can configure zero retention.
[21:45] Priya Singh: Can we set different SLOs per route? like checkout 150ms p95, recommendations 400ms?
[21:54] Jordan Lee: Yes per-route SLOs are supported and the router uses them to auto-select lower latency models when needed.
[22:20] [23:00] Tom Rinehart: If we go with Hosted for dev, what rate limits apply to trial accounts?
[23:10] Alex Chen: Trial accounts have conservative default quotas, but we can temporarily lift them for onboarding tests. For prod you pick committed capacity or Dedicated.
[23:38] Priya Singh: Question on billing on Dedicated — if we overrun committed capacity in a month, how is overage billed?
[23:48] Jordan Lee: Overage is billed at predetermined per-token or per-GPU rates. You can also configure burst commitments to reduce overage charges.
[24:10] [24:40] Maya Patel: returning to Optimize: we ran a quick model selection for your prompt set — recommended A-variant for checkout and B-variant for recommendations. I'll send the export for your team to validate.
[25:05] Tom Rinehart: Good. Can you share a trimmed video of the console parts we looked at?
[25:15] Alex Chen: Yup we'll send a 5-min clip of the key flows + the sim output.
[25:35] Priya Singh: One more technical — will latency spikes from GC in the runtime cause tokens to queue?
[25:45] Maya Patel: The runtime isolates GC pauses with memory pools and pre-allocated buffers; we also smooth token dispatch via continuous batching to reduce spike impact.
[26:10] [27:00] Tom Rinehart: What's the typical SLA for Dedicated on p95 latency?
[27:12] Alex Chen: SLA is uptime and a latency covariance target; specific p95 numbers are part of contract commitments — we'll provide examples from similar customers.
[27:40] Priya Singh: If we need data residency EU-only, is that supported?
[27:50] Jordan Lee: Yes hosted EU regions and private in-region installs are supported. We'll mark that requirement in the follow up.
[28:05] Luis Gomez: For procurement — we'll need standard security docs, DPA, and vendor questionnaires.
[28:16] Alex Chen: We'll share the security pack. Also happy to arrange a legal/procurement brief.
[28:35] [29:00] Maya Patel: Demo wrap-up — console patterns recap: use project keys as billing anchor, org keys for global policies, configure priority lanes for critical routes, and use burst buckets for controlled campaign spikes.
[29:32] Tom Rinehart: That matches what we hoped. Next is to size nodes and see pricing impact.
[29:45] Alex Chen: We'll do that. Jordan, anything else on the technical follow-up?
[29:52] Jordan Lee: I'll prepare a short runbook for canary best practices and the CSV simulator template.
[30:10] Priya Singh: Please include the pre-warm API examples.
[30:18] Jordan Lee: Will do.
[30:40] [31:00] Tom Rinehart: Ok quick timeline — we aim to decide by 2025-11-14 for infra commitment. If we go Dedicated we'll want a 2-week pilot.
[31:20] Alex Chen: Sounds good. We'll align pricing and availability and get the pilot plan ready.
[31:35] Sara Albright: One last product question — do you support feature flags at route level?
[31:44] Maya Patel: Yes feature flags tied to routing rules are supported. You can enable/disable model variants per project.
[32:05] Luis Gomez: Action: we'll draft security questions and share with Alex.
[32:12] Tom Rinehart: Thanks everyone this was helpful.
[32:20] Alex Chen: Thank you — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[32:30] [End of recording — remainder of call was wrap and scheduling]

Notes: occasional transcript errors present (e.g., "K V cash" for KV cache in one auto-transcribe), filler words, overlapping talk. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/console-clip-acadia (demo clip), https://redwood.example.com/optimize-reco-acadia (optimize export), and a sizing spreadsheet to be shared via email.
